Navigating the AI Reckoning with RBC Capital's Software Equity Research Team58 min35 insights2026-11-17
▶ Watch on YouTube
Dan Nathan sits down with RBC Capital's software analysts (Rishi, Matt Hedberg, Matt Swanson) ahead of RBC's TMT conference: software has lost its role as the 'anti-AI trade' and now sells off in lockstep with Nvidia-driven tech weakness, but the team argues the 'SaaS apocalypse' fears were overdone (Microsoft's recovery, AI-native companies still buying incumbent software) and that 2027's key catalyst is forward-looking AI metrics (ServiceNow AI ACV, Dynatrace consumption, Okta agent identity) finally showing up in P&L growth, with ad tech shifting toward SSPs, CTV and in-app formats.

Software sentiment: no longer the anti-AI hedge 6

Microsoft's rebound and the Copilot leg 5
Investors got Microsoft wrong on three counts at peak SaaS-apocalypse fear: the 'vibe code your own Excel' threat, the idea Azure was losing the hyperscale cloud war (it was just disciplined on capex and stayed cash-flow positive while peers burned cash and tapped markets), and the view that Office Copilot had failed.
contrarian🗣 Rishi (RBC software analyst)conviction: highMicrosoftAzureOffice CopilotExcel
So what: Microsoft's earlier 30%+ drawdown was narrative-driven; capex discipline is a differentiator vs. cash-burning hyperscalers.
“we're just going to vibe code our own Excel, which is a terrible idea” ▶ 11:19
Office Copilot is turning: engagement metrics and net paid adds are improving, the Office line has already accelerated, and customer feedback is meaningfully better than a year ago after Satya Nadella stepped back into the product.
data_point🗣 Rishi (RBC software analyst)conviction: highMicrosoftOffice CopilotSatya Nadella
So what: Copilot ARPU uplift on roughly half a billion paid Office users is the next leg of the Microsoft story beyond Azure.
“customer feedback to office co-pilot is meaningfully better than it was even a year ago” ▶ 12:08
Microsoft's early decision to build Copilot model-agnostic (usable with any LLM, including open-weight models) lets it orchestrate multiple models simultaneously; model orchestration - picking the right model for the right job cost-efficiently - is a key bull case for Microsoft and other incumbents.
thesis🗣 Rishi (RBC software analyst)conviction: highMicrosoftOpenAIopen-weight modelsCopilot
So what: Reduced OpenAI dependence lowers model-cost and vendor risk; orchestration becomes an incumbent moat.
“this is a really important bullcase for Microsoft and others is that model orchestration piece” ▶ 13:44
Cloud growth has reaccelerated across hyperscalers: Azure roughly high-30s/40% year-over-year, GCP around 100% off a smaller base, and AWS reaccelerating after bottoming around 12-13%.
data_point🗣 Dan Nathan (host)conviction: mediumAzureGCPAWSAmazonGoogle

Microsoft likely stays a defensive holding into 2027 given its duration; the baton would pass away from it only when investors see live, non-custom-built knowledge-worker AI use cases, shifting focus from AI infrastructure (where cracks are already appearing) to applications.
prediction🗣 Rishi (RBC software analyst)conviction: mediumMicrosoftAI infrastructure

The AI Domino Effect Begins33 min26 insights2026-11-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Guy Adami and Dan Nathan argue that Jensen Huang's exit, plus a WSJ report on pressure to push GPU sales through circular financing and neocloud backstops, is starting a chain reaction in the AI trade. They expect neoclouds such as CoreWeave to lose their Nvidia safety net, a weak or pulled Nvidia guide on its first post-Jensen earnings, a strained ~$1.5T Anthropic IPO, and unwinds in crowded secondary AI trades (semis, memory, Palo Alto, Cisco, Bitcoin), with Apple and Microsoft as the only places to hide.

Nvidia's first post-Jensen earnings 7
Nvidia reports its first-ever earnings without Jensen Huang, with the CFO of the last 13 years as interim CEO; options imply a ~10% move. Consensus expects ~90% growth this year slowing to ~70% next year, and the stock trades at ~$160, or ~17x earnings.
data_point🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNvidiaJensen
So what: Set up for a binary earnings event; implied vol of ~10% likely understates the tail if guidance is pulled.
Nathan argues valuation offers no floor: Nvidia's gross margin rose from ~55% in 2022 to an expected ~73%, and if customers now gain pricing power, margins compress and the 'cheap' multiple is illusory.
thesis🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNvidia
So what: Watch gross-margin guidance as the key variable; margin compression would re-rate the stock lower despite a low P/E.
“So if all this really means that for the first time ever their customers have pricing power then margins are going lower.” ▶ 5:40
Adami disagrees with Gene Munster's view that Nvidia still 'holds all the cards'; he believes customers can now push back, and historically margin deterioration is a reason to exit a stock and not look back.
contrarian🗣 Guy Adamiconviction: mediumNvidiaGene Munster
So what: Treat any gross-margin decline as a sell signal rather than a dip to buy.
Both hosts expect Nvidia's guidance to be so wide 'you could drive a truck through it' or to be pulled entirely; Nathan says the new CEO and board face liability if they guide to numbers they know they cannot hit, and that if guidance is pulled the stock cannot rally.
prediction🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNvidia
So what: Asymmetric downside into the print; Q&A content and whether a Q&A happens at all matter more than reported numbers.
“If they pull the guidance, there's no way the stock rallies people.” ▶ 26:40
Adami compares Nvidia to GE under Jack Welch, where quarter-after-quarter earnings massaging to beat by a penny was uncovered after Welch left; he expects similar revelations now that Jensen, the 'puppet master', is gone.
framework🗣 Guy Adamiconviction: mediumNvidiaGeneral ElectricJack Welch
So what: Post-founder transitions often reveal accounting or channel issues; watch for restatements, inventory and receivables changes.
Nathan cites Cisco's long run of beating by a penny and its November 2007 miss and guide-down, which marked the top for tech, as a template for a single bellwether guide-down ending a tech cycle.
framework🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: mediumCiscoJohn Chambers

Technically, Adami sees Nvidia testing its prior all-time high (~$148, January 2025) as support after falling from ~$240 two months earlier; he says the stock's decline was inevitable and the worst may not be over.
thesis🗣 Guy Adamiconviction: mediumNvidia
So what: ~$148 is the key support level; a break would signal further downside.
Circular financing and neocloud fallout 6
A Wall Street Journal report says Jensen pressed the CFO to push more cash out (via a ~$600 billion bank lending facility and deals run by his son-in-law) so buyers would purchase GPUs and keep pace with wafer orders, which Nathan says must be weighing on forward guidance.
data_point🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNvidiaWall Street Journal
So what: Suggests end demand was partly financed by Nvidia itself; organic demand may be lower than reported orders imply.
Nvidia funds neoclouds that exist mainly to buy its chips, then backstops up to 25% of their compute if it goes unused, which the hosts say has been a red flag since August.
causal🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNvidiaNeoclouds
So what: Neocloud demand is not arm's-length; if Nvidia's backstop capacity shrinks, neocloud credit and equity are exposed.
Nathan says neoclouds will be the 'Global Crossings, Nortels and Lucents' of this cycle: if Nvidia cannot absorb excess capacity and they cannot raise capital to buy chips to rent out, they go away, especially given their debt loads.
prediction🗣 Dan Nathanconviction: highNeocloudsGlobal CrossingNortelLucent

Rational Security: The “Nightmare on Pennsylvania Avenue” Edition88 min23 insights2026-11-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Lawfare's Rational Security panel (Scott R. Anderson, Julia Curley, Ben Wittes, Roger Parloff) dissects the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after an affair with Alice Wong, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer executive US intelligence reportedly tied to China's MSS, framing it as both a counterintelligence breach and a key-person/succession risk for the most important company in the US economy. They also cover Thomas Massie's tabled impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (Iran war, boat strikes) and Judge Chutkin's TRO blocking Trump's 250-foot triumphal arch, with implications for how a Democratic Congress will use appropriations riders and oversight.

Economics Professor on How to Fix The British Economy | Sir Paul Collier86 min39 insights2026-11-16

Oxford economist Sir Paul Collier tells Peter McCormack that Britain's ~zero per-capita growth is a threat to democracy, caused mainly by extreme centralization in the Treasury, over-financialization (domestic share of UK savings invested at home down from ~half to 4%), and powerless, broke local government. His fixes: devolve money and power to regional mayors, split the Treasury with a Ministry of Economy, rebuild local risk capital for scale-ups, tax land appreciation, cut energy costs and net-zero zeal, lower youth wages and fix NEET/benefit incentives, and rejoin a European security club.

Laura Shin hosts Securitize president Brett Redford and SEC Trading & Markets director Jamie Selway on why 67 companies opted out of tokenized trading on OKX ICE's tokenized securities venue (TSV) under the SEC's 5-year innovation exemption: rushed notices and anti-tokenization campaigns (with alleged Nasdaq involvement) drove knee-jerk opt-outs, while the SEC defends issuer consent, no synthetics, volume caps, and targets a 2027 rule proposal; Securitize contrasts its broker-dealer/issuer-sponsored model now at 47 names.

Innovation exemption design 7
The SEC's innovation exemption, issued September 17, is a 5-year conditional exemption letting TSVs trade tokenized exchange-listed stocks via permissioned automated market makers without registering as exchanges or brokers.
data_point🗣 Laura Shin (host)conviction: highSECTSVAMM
So what: Creates a new class of on-chain secondary venues for US equities.
The exemption caps each TSV at 25 basis points of volume share in the most liquid stocks and 2.5% in less liquid stocks, and the 5-year term is meant to force permanent rulemaking.
data_point🗣 Jamie Selway (SEC)conviction: highSECTSV
So what: Volume caps limit near-term disruption to incumbent exchanges and market makers.
The SEC excluded synthetics and required tokens to carry all rights of the security because the digital-asset community it consulted wanted securities entitlements, not derivatives; synthetics would also pull in security-based swap rules.
causal🗣 Jamie Selway (SEC); Brett Redfordconviction: highSECsynthetic tokenssecurity-based swaps
So what: Onshore tokenized equities will be real-share-backed; synthetic exposure stays offshore for now.
Selway would not rule out tokenized derivatives later, noting single-stock and 2x single-stock ETFs already offer compliant synthetic exposure, and hopes to move from exemption to rulemaking within about a year.

So what: A path for tokenized synthetic products exists if brokers request it.

Capital Allocators · Ted Seides 1 episode(s) · 32 insights

Paul Enright: Single-Manager Hedge Funds, Pod Shops, and Equity Research in the Age of AI60 min32 insights2026-11-18
▶ Watch on YouTube
Former Viking and Jain Global PM Paul Enright contrasts single-manager hedge funds (unit of production = an exceptional idea, slugging percentage) with multi-manager pod shops (unit = a portfolio, batting average plus leverage), argues that since 2011 roughly two-thirds of stock returns came from multiple changes that the earnings-obsessed industry cannot systematize, and lays out how AI should automate short half-life research while humans build crystallized long half-life knowledge. He now favors a concentrated public/private best-ideas vehicle, citing Coatue's CTEK as the most innovative recent product.
Single-manager vs pod-shop production models · 7Scale advantages of multi-managers · 3Multiple expansion as the unexploited edge · 6Where edge lives now: battleground stocks · 5AI in the research process and team design · 6Public/private best-ideas vehicles · 5
Single-manager vs pod-shop production models 7
At a single-manager fund the chief unit of production is an exceptional idea, while at a multi-manager it is a portfolio, so the top 10 portfolios drive a pod shop's returns the way the top 10 ideas drive a single manager's.
framework🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highsingle managermulti-manager
So what: Allocators should evaluate the two models on different units: idea quality vs portfolio-construction and risk-management quality.
“If you're a multi-manager, the idea is a component, but it's not the product. The product is the portfolio itself.” ▶ 1:16
Multi-manager quality control happens ex post through risk management that 'recalls' or discontinues portfolios, whereas single managers quality-control ideas ex ante like Apple perfecting an iPhone before launch.
framework🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: mediummulti-managerApple
So what: Explains why pod shops cut PMs quickly: the risk system, not upfront vetting, is the quality filter.
Multi-manager analysts have a harder job than single-manager analysts because they must research, generate ideas, and package them into themed baskets ('sleeves'), effectively doing part of the portfolio management.
thesis🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highmulti-manager
So what: Talent at pod shops needs portfolio-construction skills, not just stock picking.
Single managers risk hidden correlation because ideas vetted independently may all be the same bet, while multi-managers risk diluting their five best ideas by sizing them like everything else.
framework🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highsingle managermulti-manager
So what: Useful diligence check: test single managers for factor concentration and pod shops for best-idea dilution.
Enright says the biggest surprise inside a pod shop was how vital breadth and diversification are: multi-manager is a batting-average business driven by volatility and Sharpe, while single manager is a slugging-percentage business driven by long-short spread and gross/net.
data_point🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highmulti-manager
So what: Different return engines mean different failure modes and suitability within an allocator's portfolio.
“It's a batting average business and single manager is much more of a slugging percentage best ideas for most.” ▶ 10:01
Pod shops lever lower-alpha, lower-risk idea packages heavily, so on an unlevered apples-to-apples basis their returns would not match an exceptional concentrated idea.
causal🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: mediummulti-managerleverage
So what: Pod-shop returns are partly a leverage product, exposing them to funding and crowding risk.
Concentration, volatility and leverage cannot coexist; a fund must pick at most two, and being levered, concentrated and volatile guarantees blowups.
framework🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highleverage
So what: A simple screen for spotting fragile hedge fund risk profiles.
“you can't have concentration, volatility, and leverage together. You're dead.” ▶ 16:49
Scale advantages of multi-managers 3
When Enright entered the industry there was more talent than capital (Tiger was the only game in town in the late 90s); multi-managers now have more capital than talent, making them the magnet for talent.
causal🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highTigerVikingmulti-manager
So what: Capital-rich pod shops win the talent war, pressuring single managers' ability to recruit and retain.
Scale lets pod shops run a center book on top of PM portfolios, which Enright calls almost pure margin layered on breadth.
thesis🗣 Paul Enrightconviction: highcenter bookmulti-manager
So what: Center-book economics are a key structural advantage of the largest platforms.
“it's almost like it's like almost pure margin on top of that” ▶ 13:23
Scale also wins in the data layer: large teams acquire, clean and structure data so analysts spend time analyzing rather than wrangling, and AI amplifies that advantage.

So what: AI may widen rather than narrow the gap between the largest platforms and smaller funds.
Multiple expansion as the unexploited edge 6
Enright's attribution work from 1998-2025 shows early periods were dominated by earnings growth, but from 2011-2025 roughly two-thirds of annual stock returns came from multiple expansion, with 2018 as a dramatic de-rating year.

So what: Earnings-forecasting edge explains less of returns than the industry assumes; multiple drivers deserve more research.

Two kinds of convexity: return vs exposure 4
Uve defines convexity as the gradient of a CTA's expected extra return to an equity move of either sign (a 'mod x' fit): a 15% convexity implies roughly an extra 75bp in the quarter for a 5% equity drawdown, and even zero convexity (uncorrelated) is valuable because most portfolio assets are a growth bet.
framework🗣 Uve (guest, CTA manager)conviction: highconvexityCTAscrisis alpha
So what: Gives allocators a quantifiable way to compare defensive sleeves rather than relying on correlation alone.
“although your book may look diversified, it is essentially a growth bet” ▶ 13:20
Private equity, private credit, and public credit are all strongly positively correlated with equities, so a seemingly diversified portfolio of these assets falls together in an equity drawdown, whereas CTAs tend to rise.
thesis🗣 Uve (guest, CTA manager)conviction: highprivate equityprivate creditpublic creditCTAs
So what: Private-market allocations do not diversify equity risk; true diversifiers must have zero or negative equity beta in drawdowns.
Return convexity (e.g., long bonds rallying when equities fall) is immediate but not guaranteed because it depends on the macro regime, while exposure convexity (a CTA mechanically turning short equities) is guaranteed but arrives with a one-to-two-month lag and initially loses money because a drawdown follows a rally when the CTA is long.
framework🗣 Uve (guest, CTA manager)conviction: highconvexitybondsequitiesCTAs
So what: A defensive basket needs both a 'first responder' (bonds/bond trend) and a 'second responder' (equity trend) to cover different crisis shapes.
“So actually a CTA initially will lose money from an equity exposure convexity.” ▶ 18:08

causal🗣 Uve (guest, CTA manager)conviction: highequity trendLiberation DayTrumpbonds

“the equity part of the convexity actually is just too late to the party” ▶ 31:21
CTA capital efficiency: bonds vs equities 6
Because CTAs equalize risk across asset classes at about 15% vol, they deleverage equities and lever up bonds, so a 10% CTA allocation gives only about plus/minus 3.5% equity exposure but roughly plus/minus 10% bond exposure.

So what: Funding a CTA from bonds can add net bond exposure; CTAs are a capital-efficient bond-trend overlay, not an efficient equity hedge.
“CTAs is a much more capital efficient when it comes to the bond sector than it is to the equity sector” ▶ 22:45
Moving 10% of a 40% bond allocation into a CTA yields adaptive bond exposure of roughly 40% when bonds trend well and 20% when they trend badly, but the same 10% does little for the 60% equity sleeve.
data_point🗣 Uve (guest, CTA manager)conviction: high60/40 portfolioCTAsbonds

Faster trend systems commit less capital on average: a slow trend holds about 60% of full exposure in a sustained trend (about plus/minus 3.5% equity exposure per 10% allocation), while fast trend averages around 30% commitment (about plus/minus 2%).

Flirting with Models · Corey Hoffstein 1 episode(s) · 27 insights

Richard Falk-Wallace – Risk Models for the Front Office with Arcana (S8E1)67 min27 insights2026-11-16
▶ Watch on YouTube
Richard Falk-Wallace (ex-JP Morgan restructuring, Silver Point, Viking, Citadel PM), founder of Arcana, tells Corey Hoffstein that factor-risk and portfolio-construction discipline is migrating from the back office to the fundamental PM's desk because pods have won on risk-adjusted returns, factor volatility has risen, and alpha is scarcer. He details why even correct factor bets drag Sharpe, what performance decomposition (sizing vs selection, earnings vs ex-earnings, holding-period aging) reveals, how to treat transient themes like AI, and why buy-in to any solid risk model matters more than last-mile model refinements.
Why risk tooling moved to the PM desk · 5Factor exposure as Sharpe drag · 7Performance decomposition patterns · 5Risk model design and themes like AI · 6Signal vs noise and AI tooling · 4
Why risk tooling moved to the PM desk 5
Factor-risk models were historically built for the back office/risk function rather than portfolio managers; outside a handful of multi-managers with large in-house systems, most fundamental firms had only artisanal or no tooling, which is the gap Arcana targets.
thesis🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highArcanamulti-managers
So what: Signals a growing market for front-office risk/portfolio analytics vendors (Arcana vs Barra, Axioma, Wolfe) serving mid-size fundamental funds.
Three forces pushed portfolio-construction analytics upstream to PMs: multi-manager pods have won on realized risk-adjusted returns, factor volatility has secularly risen (attributed to passive, concentration and thematic concentration), and alpha has become less abundant.
causal🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highmulti-managerspassive investingfactor volatility
So what: Fundamental long/short managers without factor discipline face structural disadvantage versus pods; supports continued pod asset gathering.
The classic Tiger Cub product of delivering market returns at half the volatility (or ~1.5-2x market returns at the same vol) no longer happens at scale because the market is less alpha-rich, forcing managers to stop leaking Sharpe through avoidable mistakes.
contrarian🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumtiger cubequity long short
So what: Allocators should scrutinize concentrated long-biased hedge funds' portfolio construction, not just stock picks.
“As players get better, you can't make dumb mistakes.” ▶ 12:00
Quant investing has progressively climbed the stack of front-running fundamental investors: V1 front-ran the trading desk via price/volume, V2 front-ran fundamental data points via alternative data, and AI now begins front-running qualitative investment analysis; meanwhile fundamental investors adopt quant portfolio construction.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumAIalternative dataquant
So what: Edge in qualitative fundamental research is eroding as AI scales; fundamental managers must combine depth with portfolio-construction breadth to stay competitive.
Multi-manager platforms and the rise of SMAs let allocators build quant-like breadth by aggregating many concentrated fundamental PMs while managing aggregate factor risk centrally.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediummulti-managersSMAs
So what: SMA and multi-manager structures are becoming the industry template for combining fundamental alpha with diversification.
Factor exposure as Sharpe drag 7
Even when a PM correctly calls a factor, factor exposure drags book Sharpe toward the factor's low Sharpe; the market factor's long-run Sharpe is about 0.6-0.8 while skilled market-neutral PMs run 1-2, and roughly half of non-market factors are net detractors over time.
contrarian🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highmarket betamomentumgrowth
So what: Paying PMs for factor bets is paying for low-Sharpe beta; allocators should isolate residual returns when evaluating managers.
“you can just sort of hurt yourself even if you get the factor call right” ▶ 20:41
The number one portfolio-construction lesson fundamental investors are slowest to adopt is avoiding knowable sources of correlation: correlation is mathematically equivalent to concentration and drags Sharpe except in rare moments when all correlations go your way.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highportfolio constructioncorrelation
So what: Managers with large net beta or momentum loadings are taking unrewarded risk that will compress risk-adjusted returns.
Beta and momentum are typically the largest factor drags on Sharpe; well-performing books tend to be long momentum, and it is useful to separate accrued momentum (passively gained from winners) from bought momentum.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumbetamomentum
So what: Watch for momentum crowding in strong-performing books; a momentum reversal hits winners disproportionately.
The cleanest pod-style guardrails are a band around ex-ante predicted beta plus a minimum idiosyncratic share of variance (commonly 70-90%), optionally with single-factor variance limits; over-constraining adds complexity without benefit.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highmulti-managersidiosyncratic risk
So what: Fundamental managers can adopt two simple constraints to capture most of the pod risk benefit.
Big pods say 'there's no gold star for a higher idio': PMs must clear an idiosyncratic-share threshold, after which they are judged purely on P&L, not on having the tightest book.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediummulti-managers
So what: Explains pod behavior: books cluster just above idio thresholds rather than maximally neutralized.
“there's no gold star for having the tightest book” ▶ 56:42
Long-only benchmark-relative managers are effectively market-neutral versus the benchmark, yet institutional dynamics mean owning a benchmark-weight 7% Nvidia position still requires a big IC debate; concentration and liquidity limits push them into structural size and other factor tilts that can drive half to two-thirds of relative performance if uncontrolled.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumNvidialong onlytracking error
So what: Mega-cap concentration creates large unintended factor bets in active long-only funds, a source of underperformance versus benchmarks.
A random selection of stocks from a coverage universe naturally produces a high-idio, market-neutral-capable book; factor problems arise from non-random biases that are usually correlated with themes the PM likes.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediummarket neutral
So what: High factor loadings reveal a manager's embedded thematic bias, useful for allocator due diligence.
Performance decomposition patterns 5
Across managers, selection returns are far more stable than sizing returns; sizing P&L is about a coin flip in absolute terms and almost always a Sharpe-ratio drag.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highsizingselection
So what: Allocators and PMs should be skeptical of conviction-weighted sizing; equal-ish sizing may improve risk-adjusted returns.
“It's as likely as not that you lost money as you made money on sizing.” ▶ 30:44
PMs show persistent idiosyncratic patterns around earnings (e.g., consistently making money into earnings and losing on the way out), and a PM's earnings hit rate is often eerily close to their overall residual hit rate.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumearningshit rate
So what: Earnings hit rate is a quick proxy for a PM's overall residual skill.
Holding-period aging analysis often shows contrarian PMs consistently losing money in the first 15-30 days of a position before the thesis pays off, a persistent and correctable timing bias.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumtrade timing
So what: Contrarian managers can improve returns by scaling into positions more slowly.
The easiest way to improve performance is not to find new skill but to isolate and cut what a PM is consistently bad at while preserving what they are good at; only a handful of firms systematically iterate on this.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highmulti-managers
So what: Process discipline at scale compounds into differentiated outcomes, particularly in levered low-alpha portfolios.
“often the easiest way to improve performance is to just isolate those things that you're consistently bad at” ▶ 31:57
Distinguishing PM skill from noise in residual hit rates takes roughly two years for market-neutral books turning over 8 to low-20s times a year; higher-volatility books need longer, lower-vol or quant books less.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumSharpe ratiomulti-managers
So what: Sets a realistic evaluation horizon for allocators and pod risk managers before judging a PM.
Risk model design and themes like AI 6
The core workhorse factors (growth, value, quality, momentum, beta, industry) persist across decades even as their statistical significance rotates; fundamental-attribute factors handle nonlinear risks better than time-series factors, e.g., homebuilder rate risk is best neutralized via the homebuilding industry factor rather than a 10-year rates factor.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highhome builder10-yearfactor models
So what: Hedging rate shocks in housing names via sector exposure is more reliable than relying on historical rate correlations.
A practical way to measure true AI exposure is to compute each stock's residual beta to the residual returns of a bank AI basket (JP Morgan, MSI, Goldman), but such time-series measures are volatile: in the past week Nvidia flipped from an AI long to an AI short.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumNvidiaJP MorganGoldmanAI
So what: AI-theme exposure is unstable; Nvidia's shifting role in AI baskets signals rotation within AI trades.
“Nvidia itself, right, has flipped from being an AI long to an AI short.” ▶ 50:24
Adding more factors, shorter covariance windows, PCA or transient thematic factors almost monotonically raises a risk model's R-squared but reduces simplicity, persistence and usability; the biggest differentiator is firm-wide buy-in to any solid fundamental cross-sectional model (Barra, Axioma, Wolfe, Arcana).
contrarian🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highBarraAxiomaWolfeArcana
So what: Vendor choice matters less than process adoption; implementation and buy-in drive value.
“the most effective split is going to be just whatever model your firm buys into.” ▶ 54:42
Crowding is a widely added reference factor; widespread factor neutralization does not by itself create directional crowding because risk models don't tell PMs which side of a pair (e.g., Visa vs Mastercard, Ford vs GM) to take.
contrarian🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumcrowdingVisaMastercardFordGM
So what: Crowding risk from shared risk models is lower than feared at the single-stock level, though factor neutralization is common.
Arcana offers prediction-market-based exposures to a Democratic policy sweep as a thematic risk factor, alongside bank thematic baskets.
data_point🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: lowArcanaprediction markets
So what: Policy-event exposures derived from prediction markets are entering mainstream risk tooling.
Whether to neutralize a theme like AI power demand depends on how much it overlaps core factor exposures, its volatility contribution to the book, and whether the PM judges it worth the vol it adds.
framework🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumAI power demand
So what: Thematic bets that overlap momentum/beta are disguised factor bets and will drag long-term Sharpe.
Signal vs noise and AI tooling 4
Factors are the largest driver of a fundamental portfolio's outcome (often most of its R-squared), orders of magnitude more important than a single research note, sell-side block-trade flag or alt-data point that PMs spend time on.
thesis🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: highfactor riskBloomberg
So what: Fundamental PMs should prioritize risk/factor management over incremental information gathering.
“factors are huge. They're waves in the ocean of stock picking” ▶ 39:07
Anecdotally, PMs most dialed in on factor risk and portfolio construction tend to have the best returns, though Arcana has not studied this systematically.
anecdote🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: lowArcana
So what: Use risk-process maturity as a qualitative manager-selection signal.
AI interfaces (on-platform LLM agents, MCPs, APIs, Excel plug-ins) create a Jevons paradox in risk analytics: lower cost of analysis leads PMs to run far more analyses rather than replacing existing workflows.
prediction🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumMCPJevons paradoxAI
So what: Demand for risk/analytics data and tooling should expand as AI lowers usage friction.
“It just Jebans paradoxes everything about this world.” ▶ 1:02:17

prediction🗣 Richard Falk-Wallaceconviction: mediumportfolio construction

Adoption lag of proven medical breakthroughs 5
Ether anesthesia (1846) spread worldwide within days of journal publication with no clinical-trial gate, yet surgical mortality initially worsened because surgeons operated more aggressively without understanding germs; only Joseph Lister's antisepsis, applying Pasteur's germ theory from the 1860s, made surgery 'limitless'.

So what: Incumbent professional resistance, not evidence, often sets the adoption curve for innovations that implicate current practice; model slower uptake when a product implies practitioners were wrong.

Spotting a scam: three layers of reality 4
Mauriello's three-layer framework: (1) measurable objective reality, (2) future-facing stories grounded in it, and (3) self-conception or vision; layers two and three must eventually reckon with layer one, especially for products that can be measured and repeated, like medical tests.

So what: A diligence lens: story-premium businesses work in fashion or luxury but fail where outputs are scientifically testable.
